newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Wary Taiwan pins hopes on HK leader-designate.
newsitem.headline: Wary Taiwan pins hopes on HK leader-designate.

text.p: Taiwan congratulated Hong Kong's newly selected leader-in-waiting on Wednesday, saying shipping mogul Tung Chee-hwa, as chief executive, would profoundly affect the territory's future under Chinese rule.

But analysts and citizens remained deeply sceptical that the British colony's quickening steps toward Chinese sovereignty in 1997 could point the way to the estranged island's own reunion with the communist mainland.

"We would like to congratulate Mr Tung's high-vote victory," the cabinet's Mainland Affairs council said. "Mr Tung's victory will have a profound influence on Hong Kong's peaceful transition and its freedom and prosperity."
Taipei believed Tung, chosen in Hong Kong on Wednesday by a Beijing-selected panel of 400 Hong Kong people, would have "excellent achievements" in his five-year term, it said.
The warmth of Taiwan's statement contrasted sharply with a November assessment by council spokesman, Kao Koong-lian, slamming the Beijing-orchestrated process as "a big joke".
The new statement held out hope that Tung could help ease deep strains between China and Taiwan, regarded by Beijing as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949.
"Mutually beneficial Taiwan-Hong Kong relations have a great importance on economic prosperity and social stability in Hong Kong, Taiwan and mainland China," it said.
Semi-official Taiwan-China talks collapsed in 1995, leaving many issues on Taiwan's future ties with Hong Kong unresolved.
Taiwan officials said Tung, who takes office on July 1, was familiar with the island through his shipping operations.
The British colony's handover to Beijing is widely seen as increasing pressure for Taiwan's own reunification with China, something both sides espouse though under very different terms.
Taiwan insists that reunification can only be realised after China -- like Taiwan -- becomes democratic.
China has vowed to let Hong Kong keep its capitalist system for 50 years under a one country, two systems model, which Beijing says then can be applied to its bigger aim of regaining Taiwan.
Tung's selection, widely seen as having been stage managed by Beijing, left Taiwan political analysts deeply sceptical.

"If Beijing can realise the one-country, two-systems promise and maintain the stability and prosperity of Hong Kong, of course it will be easier for Beijing to handle the Taiwan issue," said Taipei political economist Ma Kai.
"But it is impossible to put Taiwan in Hong Kong's position as they exist under very different conditions."
Ma pointed to the wide gap between Taiwan's political and economic autonomy and Britain's colonial rule of Hong Kong.
A sampling of Taiwan people said reunification would be rocky if Beijing sought to use Hong Kong's return as a model.
"Nobody believes communist China's one-country, two-systems model will work out in the end. Hong Kong won't be the same Hong Kong in a few years," said bullion executive Wang Li-ling.

"I don't think it can apply that model to Taiwan," she said. "In Hong Kong, only dozens of people protested against the undemocratic election today. You can imagine how many people would take to the streets here. It wouldn't be the same."
Local media also raised doubts.
"Today is the day when Hong Kong officially steps into the post-1997 era," the United Daily News said in an editorial.
"Is the return (to China) a national reunion or a disaster? Is 'two systems' a political promise or a lie?"
